testCases.name: test_case_14
testCases.input: what are computed and captured signals in online evaluation?
testCases.actualOutput:
In online evaluation we rely on two kinds of information to tell us whether the chatbot is behaving as we expect: captured signals and computed signals.

A captured signal is something that the system already records as the user interacts with the bot. You don’t have to do any extra processing—just store the value that’s produced. The classic examples are the thumbs‑up or thumbs‑down feedback a user clicks after a response, the latency of a reply, or the cost incurred for handling a request. Because these data points are emitted directly by the user interface or the runtime environment, we simply capture them and log them (for instance, in a tool like LangSmith) without any further calculation.

A computed signal, on the other hand, is a metric that isn’t emitted automatically; you have to derive it from the conversation data. To obtain it you set up an evaluator that processes the chat logs and produces a score. A typical example is a “faithfulness” or “hallucination” metric that measures how accurately the bot’s answer reflects the source information. Since the raw chat alone doesn’t contain that score, you send the exchange to an online evaluator, which runs the necessary algorithm and returns the computed value. This requires building a pipeline that calculates the metric each time a new interaction occurs.

So, captured signals are directly observed and stored (like thumbs up/down, latency, cost), while computed signals are derived by running an additional evaluation step (such as faithfulness or hallucination scores) on the logged conversation. Both types together give you a complete picture of how the deployed chatbot is performing.

testCases.name: test_case_8
testCases.input: what does it mean for a benchmark to get saturated?
testCases.actualOutput:
Sure, let’s break down what “benchmark saturation” means in plain language.  

When researchers first introduce a benchmark—say a set of math problems or a question‑answering test—no model has seen it before, so the scores are usually low and there’s a lot of room to tell the models apart. As the community builds more capable language models, those models get better and better at the same benchmark. Eventually, the scores of many different systems start clustering at the top end—often in the mid‑90 percent range for things like GSM‑8K or MMLU. At that point the benchmark can no longer serve its original purpose, which is to discriminate between stronger and weaker models. Because every model is getting essentially the same high mark, the test has become “saturated.”  

When saturation happens, the benchmark is typically retired: it’s taken out of active use because it no longer provides useful signal about relative model quality. Then a new benchmark is introduced, and the cycle repeats—new benchmark, low initial scores, gradual improvement, and finally saturation again.  

So, in short, a benchmark is said to be saturated when it has been solved so well by most current models that it can’t meaningfully differentiate their capabilities any more, prompting the community to move on to a fresh, more challenging test.
